newsitem.title: INDIA: Indian banks flush with funds, search for outlets.
newsitem.headline: Indian banks flush with funds, search for outlets.

text.p: Indian banks, saddled with a pile of excess funds and poor demand for credit, are looking around for new ways to use their money, analysts and bankers said on Thursday.
They said the bulk of this cash was being invested in short-term securities, pulling interest rates down.

"The very fact that more than 86 billion rupees ($2.4 billion) was chasing short-term assets at auctions yesterday reflects the degree of liquidity in the banking system," said Aashish Pitale, manager of debt research at ICICI Securities and Finance Company (I-Sec).
"Banks are sitting on a pile of money and wondering what to do as there is little demand," said the treasury head of a European bank, who declined to be named.
"There is a lot of uncertainty... Nobody is able to take a long-term view. Most of us (bankers) hope that this is only a passing phase and that demand will pick up soon," he said.

In two separate auctions conducted on Wednesday, one for 364-day treasury bills and the other for four-day repos of government securities, the Reserve Bank of India (RBI) received bids totalling 86.30 billion rupees.
The yield on the 364-day treasury bill fell to 10.12 percent at Wednesday's fortnightly auction from the 10.35 percent maintained since December 4.
Rates also fell in the repos auction to 4.90 percent from 5.0 percent earlier this month.
Other short-term interest rates are also at unusually low levels currently with overnight rates below one percent.
The yield on the 91-day treasury bill fell to 8.10 percent at the weekly auction held last Friday, down from 8.14 percent and 8.19 percent at preceding auctions.
The European bank's head of treasury said banks were investing in short-term assets hoping that demand for credit would pick up later in the year.
I-Sec's Pitale said the demand for short-term securities indicated that market operators were uncertain about longer-term liquidity.
"The current yield curve reflects this...it is steep at the shorter end and flattens out at the longer end," he said.
The yield curve should normally reflect a pick-up in yield over longer maturities as longer term investments typically carry more risks.

"The whole problem is that demand for bank credit is not picking up," said Amit Rajpal, banking analyst at Prime Broking. "The credit figures for most of the banks are at the same levels as at the end of last year (March 31, 1996)."
Banks' problems had been compounded by the fact that deposits have grown rapidly this year.
RBI data show that bank deposits grew by 412.46 billion rupees in 1996/97 (April-March) until January 3, 1997, against 201.28 billion rupees in the corresponding period the previous year.
Bank credit, on the other hand, grew only by 92.25 billion in that period against 273.52 billion previous year.
Bankers said they were uncertain when credit would pick up.
